# Hypotheses for sexual selection

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.25\linewidth]{images/spl_ast.png}
\end{figure}  

**Sexual selection**: Differential success in mating or fertilization as a result of preferences in one sex for traits in the other sex

1) **Good genes hypothesis**: Plumage & courtship give honest signals of genetic quality

2) **Direct benefits hypothesis**: Ornaments communicate ability to provide resources &/or protection 

3) **Arbitrary choice hypothesis**: If females prefer a trait, they might select males with the trait to increase chances of sons with the trait  

\hfill \tiny ([*Astrapia splendidissima*](https://birdsoftheworld-org.proxy.birdsoftheworld.org/bow/species/splast1/cur/introduction))

# Experimental evidence for mate choice: tail length

- *E. progne* are **polygynous**: each male has multiple female mates)
- Female widowbirds prefer elongated tails (a type of **ornament**, i.e. a physical trait used to attract mates)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.75\linewidth]{images/widowbird.png}
\end{figure}  

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OPI-9oi19gQ

\hfill \tiny ([*Euplectes progne*](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/199096141); Andersson 1982)

# Experimental evidence for mate choice: UV color

- Male Bluethroats (*Luscinia svecica*) were left untreated (top), rubbed with baby oil (middle), or rubbed with sunblock (bottom)
- Birds treated with sunblock had lower mating success

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/bluethroat.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([ML182455611](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/182455611); Johnsen et al. 1998)

# Male mate choice matters, too

- Male Rock Sparrows (*Petronia petronia*) prefer females with larger breast patches

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.9\linewidth]{images/rocksp.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny ([ML43010621](https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/43010621); Griggio et al. 2005)

# Both male and female ornaments are informative

- Evidence for good genes and direct benefits hypotheses in both sexes

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.55\linewidth]{images/female_informative.png}
\end{figure}

# Extra-pair paternity is unexpectedly common

- Predictors: adult mortality (+); male contribution to care (-)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = \linewidth]{images/epp.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Griffith et al. 2002)

# Sexual selection leads to sexual dimorphism

- Types of dimorphism: **sexual dichromatism** and **sexual size dimorphism**
- Has evolved repeatedly (outer two circles below)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/ssd_phylo.jpg}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Gonzalez-Voyer et al. 2022)

# Sexual dimorphism has different causes

- Sexual size dimorphism predicted by mating system and parental care
- Sexual dichromatism predicted by parental care and extra-pair paternity

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/dimorphism.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Owens & Hartley 1998)

# Sexual dimorphism is present in fossil birds

- *Confuciusornis sanctus* fossils indicate paired, elongated retrices were a male sexual ornament

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/confusciornis.jpg}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Zhou et al. 2024)

# Natrual selection can constrain dimorphism

- Wing dimorphism in hummingbirds reduced at high altitude (but dimorphism in other traits increases)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/constraint.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Beltrán et al. 2022)

# Lekking behavior

**Leks**: Communal display grounds for promiscuous birds with no resources other than the opportunity to mate

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.55\linewidth]{images/lek_evol.png}
\end{figure}  

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cLnbiTkj1TQ

\hfill \tiny (Taylor et al. 2025)

# Hypotheses for lekking

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.25\linewidth]{images/sage_grouse.png}
\end{figure}  


1) **Hot spot model**: Males gather where they’re most likely to encounter roaming females

2) **Hot shot model**: Males gather around top males to increase their chances w/in large aggregations

3) **Female preference model**: Females prefer visiting large clusters of males

\hfill \tiny (Beehler et al. 1988; [*Centrocercus urophasianus*](https://birdsoftheworld-org.proxy.birdsoftheworld.org/bow/species/saggro/cur/introduction))

# Is the hot spot model supported in manakins?

- Prediction: males encounter more females at leks than randomly selected sites

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/hotspot_eval.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Duraes et al. 2007; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1zxJPQlFFTI&t=1s)

\normalsize
a) yes
b) no
c) maybe
